Add real light, depth and material, such as printed ink, photographed objects or optical effects, instead of a flat vector field with uniform noise.
Find a non-obvious idea about 'new music', since the step-sequencer grid is a cliché. C's concept comes from its subject; this one comes from a moodboard.
Replace default grotesks with a typographic point of view: a custom pixel system that actually animates and sounds, a contrasting face, real scale play beyond one cropped word.

tells: The concept comes from the subject. Signal corruption, a macro shot of silicon and a burning red disc together read as a computer era overheating, which ties straight to the title.
Saturated red-magenta is held across every frame. It is a bold, specific choice that works like a brand, not an accent on a neutral ground.
Real texture: scan-line tearing, a photographed chip die with grid detail and haze, and a disc with an organic, filmic surface that looks shot or composited from real material.
Type is used sparingly. The small serif 'AMC presents' sits inside the glitch layers, and the tracked wide caps of the title come with a cursor-block glyph that echoes the chip squares.
The three frames are clearly choreographed: chaos, then order (the die), then a single symbol (the sun or fire). Each frame works as a poster.
gaps: The serif credit type is close to a default editorial face and is the weakest typographic moment. A custom or more period-specific face would carry the computing idea further.
The middle frame's four-square die is quite literal. It could be pushed into a stranger, more abstract image.
The palette almost never changes. One controlled break in temperature, such as a cyan scan or a black-out, would add surprise to the sequence.

tells: The custom modular display type breaks Latin and katakana into stroke fragments ('TOKYO' resolving from glyph shards). That is a real typographic idea, not a set font.
The palette is deliberate and unusual: hot pink, acid green, violet and slate, plus grain and paper-like texture.
Frames are dense and layered (UI brackets, dot matrices, overlapping blocks) but still read clearly. Each frame has a different structure: a close crop, a framed grid, then a scattered field.
The frame-to-frame change suggests type assembling and disassembling, so the motion clearly has choreography.
gaps: The cyber-glitch Tokyo look is a well-worn genre. It needs a narrative or tonal turn that only this piece could have.
The texture is mostly flat digital grain. It lacks the photographic and material depth of A.
The third frame is close to visual noise, and the hierarchy collapses. Tighter control of density would help the type land.

tells: The live-action plate (a Dutch station platform with a poster column and a train moving past) puts the work in a real context. That is a deliberate exhibition and festival framing device.
The fluid and chrome simulation has a credited artist ('Thomas Traum'), which points to a curated multi-artist trailer, not a template.
The frames vary widely in medium (live action, then 3D sim, then flat type), which points to real editorial choreography.
But the end card is a bold red neo-grotesk name centred on light grey. It is slide-like and adds no typographic idea of its own.
gaps: There is no unifying visual idea. The frames read as a compilation of different artists rather than one authored film. It needs a connecting device, such as the poster column transforming, the way A runs on its red signal.
The end-card typography is a default bold grotesk centred on a blank ground. Integrate the type with the image or give it scale and tension.
The 3D splash is a common sim look with an unmotivated light-blue ground. It needs a specific art direction tied to the subject.

tells: Frame 1 is real location footage: a poster drop-in composited on an actual Dutch rail platform, with a train motion-blurred behind it. The perspective, daylight and grime match, which takes production, not a template.
Frame 2 is a high-end fluid/chrome simulation with iridescent highlights and secondary splash detail, credited to an actual collaborator (Thomas Traum). That is how a studio reel is put together.
The end card is a bold red grotesk on light grey, the designer's name used as a signature in a Swiss-poster idiom. Plain, but on brand.
The three frames are completely different worlds (outdoor OOH, CG sim, flat card), which points to a portfolio reel rather than one authored film.
gaps: There's no single idea holding the piece together. It plays as a compilation; C builds every frame on one concept (heat, silicon, a burning screen).
The type on the closing card is a stock bold grotesk, centred, with nothing done to it. Make the name do something, or tie it to the imagery the way C ties its title to the glowing CRT.
The palette changes from frame to frame (muted daylight, icy blue, red on grey). Commit to a colour logic across the reel.

tells: The letterforms are custom and modular, and they mix Latin with katakana-like fragments (TOKYO resolving out of broken glyphs). Type is the subject here, not a label.
The palette is a deliberate acid set: hot pink, lime, violet, and red on near-black and slate. It is unusual and stays consistent.
Frames are dense and layered: scan-line bars, pixel noise, UI-like brackets, overprinted grids and a printed texture with grain.
Each frame is built differently (macro D and target, a framed text field, a full-bleed glitch city), so there is clear choreography from glyph to word to environment.
gaps: Glitch-type is a well-worn genre. Push past the vocabulary of decoding and data-corruption to something only this subject could own.
The light is graphic and flat. C gets physical light (CRT glow, phosphor bloom), which would add depth and heat here.
Legibility peaks only once, in the TOKYO frame. Stage clearer beats of resolution so the payoff lands harder.

tells: One specific idea: the inside of a 1980s computer (silicon dies, scan-line corruption, a CRT bulging and overheating) as a literal reading of the title HALT AND CATCH FIRE.
A monochrome red palette runs across every frame, a single committed temperature that reads as heat, warning and phosphor.
Real texture and light: analogue glitch striations, a microchip-grid photomacro, a vignetted CRT glow with mottled burn.
The type is restrained and chosen: a classical serif for 'AMC presents' against tracked wide caps with a cursor block for the title. The cursor ties the type to the subject.
There is clear progression from frame to frame: noise, then structure (chip squares), then the glowing tube and the title. It reads as a choreographed build.
gaps: The middle frame (four squares centred on a grid) is the weakest poster. Give it the same density as the opening glitch frame.
The tracked-caps title is small and very restrained. A moment of expressive scale could push the climax harder.
The palette is so committed that the frames start to blur together. A single brief counter-colour beat would sharpen the rhythm.

defects: The final shot holds the OCTAVA lockup almost unchanged for about 4.8 s. Change per second drops to 6.5 and then 3.5, which is dead air.
Pairs 1/6 s apart barely differ in the staff and lockup shots. Squares pop on and off instead of moving, so there is no spacing, easing or weight to judge.
The sound has two spikes (at about 4 s and 6 s) and the rest is flat. The peak lands at about 55% and then falls into a long static tail instead of building at 60–80%.
The 'MAY' and '2027/BASEL' cards are generic outline-echo kinetic type and drop the note-square device for black grotesk type.
The 'MAY' frame is cropped at the left edge and the lockup frames repeat. These do not work as stand-alone posters.
The grain is a uniform overlay on flat fills. There is no light, falloff or depth, and the small vertical type is slightly soft at 1:1.

The audio has static sine and pluck tones with few partials and an uneven arpeggio. The noise-burst hits sound like stock elements, and there is a near-silent gap from about 8 to 9.5 s before the last hit.
gaps: Motion: the core idea (notes on a staff become the pixel wordmark) is never animated as a real transformation. The squares should physically travel, with eased flight and overshoot, from staff positions into the letterforms, instead of cutting or popping between states. The 4.8 s static end needs a reason to move.

Sound: this sounds like thin generated synth, not produced music. It needs a composed piece whose notes literally match the on-screen squares (pitch to staff row), with layered sound design, real dynamics and a peak that matches the visual climax.

Finish and system: the mid-section type cards break the square-module system. The grain is a filter, not material. Top studio work would carry the module through every shot and give the squares real light, shadow and a tactile response.
